frase_gancho.texto: Frida gathered more than four hundred fifty ex-votos, almost all of them dedicated to the Virgin of the Rosary of Talpa.

puente_narrativo.texto: Finish climbing the stone staircase and step into the studio, the brightest room in the house.

guion_corto.texto: An ex-voto is a small painting, almost always on tin, that someone commissions to give thanks to a saint or a virgin. It shows the danger the person survived, and below it a few lines tell what happened. Frida collected hundreds of them. The museum speaks of more than four hundred fifty, and most are dedicated to the Virgin of the Rosary of Talpa. She even drew her own accident in this style. As you climb, notice how misfortunes are told without fear, with the blood and the hospital in plain view. Here lies one of the roots of her painting. You will see them in the rooms and on the staircase.

guion_largo.texto:
Before going up to the studio, it is worth pausing at those small pictures hanging on the walls. They are ex-votos. The word comes from Latin and means by a promise. In Mexico, people have them painted to give thanks to a saint, to Christ or to a virgin for having saved them from danger. An illness, an accident, a fall, a fire.

Almost all of them follow the same formula. At the top appears the saint or the virgin. In the center the scene of danger is painted, with the person in peril or already saved. Below is a handwritten text that tells what happened and gives thanks. Often they were painted on commission by a neighborhood artist.

Frida collected many of these paintings. The museum speaks of more than four hundred fifty pieces, which make up one of the most complete collections in the country. According to the museum itself, most are dedicated to the Virgin of the Rosary of Talpa, a much-venerated devotion in Mexico. You will see them in the rooms and on the walls of the staircase.

Frida did not only collect them. She also made a drawing of her accident in that language, according to the museum. That way she could tell a terrible experience in a form that felt close to her.

This is one of the keys to understanding her painting. Ex-votos do not hide pain. They show hospital beds, wounds and accidents with total clarity, but they do so at a small size, with bright colors and with a text that explains. They resemble many of her paintings. Frida painted her wounded body with the same frankness.

The poet André Breton, leader of surrealism, visited Mexico in nineteen thirty-eight and said that Frida was a surrealist. She did not agree. This phrase is attributed to her: they thought I was a surrealist, but I was not; I never painted dreams, I painted my own reality. The ex-votos on this staircase help explain why. Her way of telling stories came from the Mexican popular tradition, not from the dreams of Europe.

Before going up to the studio, notice what the staircase is like. It is made of stone, and on the walls there are portraits by José María Estrada, a Mexican painter of the nineteenth century who made portraits on commission. They are also part of the popular tradition that Frida admired. So the staircase works as a small gallery of folk art.

The Virgin of the Rosary of Talpa is a much-venerated image in Talpa de Allende, in Jalisco, where pilgrims arrive from many parts of Mexico. Many ex-votos are painted to thank her for a favor. That is why it is so common to find her image among them.

Now look at one of the paintings slowly. Read the text below, look for the saint at the top and try to imagine the story it tells. Then go up. Above, the room awaits where Frida painted many of her own miracles.

texto: Find the three parts in an ex-voto: the saint at the top, the scene of danger in the center and the written text below
Read one of the texts of thanks and try to imagine the whole story
Think about how the frankness of an ex-voto resembles that of Frida’s self-portraits

texto.Collection: more than 450 ex-votos, according to the museum
texto.Main dedication: Virgin of the Rosary of Talpa
texto.Location: rooms and walls of the staircase

texto.pregunta: Myth: Frida Kahlo was a surrealist painter because she painted dreams.
texto.respuesta: Reality: She denied it. This phrase is attributed to her: they thought I was a surrealist, but I was not; I never painted dreams, I painted my own reality. Her way of telling stories is much closer to popular ex-votos.
